answers.question: What is a sealed class/interface, what are the `permits` rules, and what must permitted subclasses be (`final`/`sealed`/`non-sealed`)?
answers.shortTitle: Sealed classes/interfaces — what they are, the `permits` rules, and what permitted subclasses must be

s1_definition.profdef: A sealed class or interface, standardised in Java 17, restricts which other classes or interfaces may extend or implement it. You declare it with the `sealed` modifier and a `permits` clause listing the exact set of allowed direct subtypes. Every permitted direct subclass must itself be declared `final` (no further subclassing), `sealed` (continues the restriction with its own permits list), or `non-sealed` (reopens the hierarchy for unrestricted subclassing). This gives the author precise, compiler-enforced control over the inheritance hierarchy.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India defines the concept of an "Account" and declares by policy that only three specific account products may ever be a kind of Account: Savings, Current, and Loan — and no branch may invent a fourth type without head-office approval. Head office writes this list on an official circular. Each listed product must then state its own policy: it is either a final product that cannot be sub-divided, a further sealed product that permits only its own named variants, or an open product that any branch may extend freely. This head-office-controlled, explicitly-listed, closed family of account types is a sealed hierarchy.
s1_definition.oneliner: A sealed type uses `permits` to name exactly which types may directly extend it, and each permitted subtype must be `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A sealed class or interface, standardised in Java 17, restricts which other classes or interfaces may extend or implement it. You declare it with the `sealed` modifier and a `permits` clause listing the exact set of allowed direct subtypes. Every permitted direct subclass must itself be declared `final` (no further subclassing), `sealed` (continues the restriction with its own permits list), or `non-sealed` (reopens the hierarchy for unrestricted subclassing). This gives the author precise, compiler-enforced control over the inheritance hierarchy.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India defines the concept of an "Account" and declares by policy that only three specific account products may ever be a kind of Account: Savings, Current, and Loan — and no branch may invent a fourth type without head-office approval. Head office writes this list on an official circular. Each listed product must then state its own policy: it is either a final product that cannot be sub-divided, a further sealed product that permits only its own named variants, or an open product that any branch may extend freely. This head-office-controlled, explicitly-listed, closed family of account types is a sealed hierarchy.

**One line to remember:** A sealed type uses `permits` to name exactly which types may directly extend it, and each permitted subtype must be `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`.

sections.s2_technical:
You declare a sealed type by adding the `sealed` modifier and a `permits` clause: `public sealed interface Account permits SavingsAccount, CurrentAccount, LoanAccount { }`. This tells the compiler that the only direct subtypes of `Account` are those three named types. Any other class trying to implement `Account` is a **compile error**. This closes the hierarchy, so the author and the compiler both know the complete set of possibilities.

The **`permits` clause rules** are strict. The permitted subtypes must be **accessible** to the sealed type at compile time. In a **named module**, permitted subtypes may be in different packages of the same module. Outside modules, on the classpath, they must be in the **same package** as the sealed type. Each permitted subtype must **directly** extend or implement the sealed type; you list direct children only, not grandchildren. And every name in the `permits` list must actually exist and genuinely extend or implement the sealed type, otherwise it is a compile error.

The most important rule is what each **permitted subclass must be**. Every direct permitted subclass is required to carry exactly one of three modifiers. **`final`** means that subclass cannot itself be extended — the hierarchy ends there, which is the common choice for a concrete leaf like `SavingsAccount`. **`sealed`** means that subclass continues the sealing, so it must have its own `permits` list naming its allowed children, letting you build a multi-level closed hierarchy. **`non-sealed`** means that subclass deliberately reopens the hierarchy, so anyone may extend it without restriction — you use this when one branch of the family must remain extensible, for example a `non-sealed` base for third-party plugins. If a permitted subclass omits all three modifiers, the code does not compile.

A key detail is that you may **omit the `permits` clause** when all permitted subtypes are declared in the **same source file** as the sealed type; the compiler then infers the permitted set from the file. This is convenient for small, closed hierarchies written together. For `record` subtypes, records are implicitly `final`, so a permitted record satisfies the "must be final/sealed/non-sealed" rule automatically without you writing `final`.

The **benefits** are strong typing and exhaustiveness. Because the compiler knows the complete set of subtypes, it can verify that a `switch` over a sealed type covers every case, enabling exhaustive pattern matching without a `default` branch. It also documents intent precisely: readers know no hidden subtype exists. In banking this is powerful for modelling a fixed set of account products, transaction types, or settlement states, where accidentally adding an unhandled subtype would be a serious bug.

A senior nuance is that sealing is an **author-controlled design decision** about extensibility, distinct from `final` on a single class, because it allows a known, limited set of subtypes rather than none. Another nuance is that sealed types combine with **records and pattern matching** to form algebraic data types, giving Java a safe, closed way to model "one of these shapes." A final nuance is that the sealed constraint is enforced at **compile time and recorded in the class file** via a `PermittedSubclasses` attribute, so the JVM also rejects non-permitted subtypes at load time, making the restriction robust even against bytecode tricks.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India must model its account products as a fixed, known set: Savings, Current, and Loan. If a developer accidentally creates a fourth, unhandled account type, downstream code that computes interest or fees could silently misbehave. We need the compiler to guarantee only these three types exist. This is exactly a sealed interface with a `permits` list.

Problem 2 — Each product needs a clear extension policy. Savings and Current are concrete leaves that must never be sub-divided, so they are `final`. Loan has sub-products (home loan, car loan) that are also a closed set, so Loan is itself `sealed` with its own permits. One special product line must remain open for future third-party add-ons, so it is `non-sealed`. This demonstrates all three required modifiers.

Problem 3 — A fee calculator switches over the account type and must handle every case. Because the hierarchy is sealed, the compiler guarantees exhaustiveness, so forgetting a case is a compile error rather than a runtime surprise.

In the mini-project we define a sealed `Account` interface permitting `SavingsAccount` (final), `CurrentAccount` (final), and `LoanAccount` (sealed), where `LoanAccount` permits `HomeLoan` (final) and a `non-sealed PromoAccount` branch, then a fee calculator that pattern-switches exhaustively, logging results.

The code contains: the sealed `Account`, its permitted subtypes with each modifier, a `FeeCalculator`, and a `main`.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A sealed class or interface, standardised in Java 17, restricts which other types may extend or implement it. I declare it with the sealed modifier and a permits clause that names the exact set of allowed direct subtypes, and any other type trying to extend it is a compile error. This gives me, the author, precise and compiler-enforced control over the inheritance hierarchy, which is stronger than final on a single class because it allows a known, limited set of subtypes rather than none at all.

The permits rules are strict. The listed subtypes must be accessible to the sealed type, and I list only direct children, not grandchildren. In a named module the permitted subtypes may live in different packages of the same module, but on the plain classpath they must be in the same package as the sealed type. I can also omit the permits clause entirely if all the subtypes are declared in the same source file, in which case the compiler infers the set.

The most important rule is what each permitted subclass must be. Every direct permitted subclass must carry exactly one of three modifiers. Final means it cannot be extended further, which is the usual choice for a concrete leaf. Sealed means it continues the restriction and must have its own permits list, which lets me build a multi-level closed hierarchy. Non-sealed means it deliberately reopens that branch so anyone may extend it without restriction, which I use when one part of the family must stay extensible. If a permitted subclass omits all three, the code does not compile, and records satisfy the rule automatically because records are implicitly final.

In my banking project I model account products as a sealed Account interface permitting savings, current, and loan, where savings and current are final leaves, loan is itself sealed with its own permits for home loan and a non-sealed promo branch. The real payoff is exhaustiveness: because the compiler knows the complete set of subtypes, my fee calculator can switch over the account type with no default branch, and the compiler guarantees every case is covered. If a teammate later adds a new permitted product but forgets to handle it, the build fails immediately rather than misbehaving in production, which is exactly the safety a bank needs for a fixed set of products.

answers.question: Can a sealed class permit a subclass in a different package (module vs non-module rules)?
answers.shortTitle: Can a sealed class permit a subclass in a different package (module vs non-module rules)?

s1_definition.profdef: It depends on whether the code is in a named module. If the sealed type and its permitted subtypes belong to the same named module, the permitted subtypes may be declared in different packages of that module. If the code is on the unnamed-module classpath, all permitted subtypes must be in the same package as the sealed type. In every case the permitted subtypes must be in the same module as the sealed type — a sealed hierarchy can never span two different modules.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India's head office declares the closed list of account products. If the whole bank operates as one unified organisation (a module), head office may place the approved products in different departments (packages) across that organisation, as long as they all belong to the bank. But if the bank is just a loose collection of branches with no central organisation (the classpath), head office can only approve products kept in the very same department (same package) as the master policy document. And no matter what, an approved product can never belong to a completely different bank (a different module).
s1_definition.oneliner: Same module, different packages is allowed; classpath requires the same package; different modules is never allowed.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** It depends on whether the code is in a named module. If the sealed type and its permitted subtypes belong to the same named module, the permitted subtypes may be declared in different packages of that module. If the code is on the unnamed-module classpath, all permitted subtypes must be in the same package as the sealed type. In every case the permitted subtypes must be in the same module as the sealed type — a sealed hierarchy can never span two different modules.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India's head office declares the closed list of account products. If the whole bank operates as one unified organisation (a module), head office may place the approved products in different departments (packages) across that organisation, as long as they all belong to the bank. But if the bank is just a loose collection of branches with no central organisation (the classpath), head office can only approve products kept in the very same department (same package) as the master policy document. And no matter what, an approved product can never belong to a completely different bank (a different module).

**One line to remember:** Same module, different packages is allowed; classpath requires the same package; different modules is never allowed.

sections.s2_technical:
The sealed-class rule for subtype location was designed to balance encapsulation with practicality. The fixed, universal part is that **all permitted subtypes must be in the same module as the sealed type**. A sealed hierarchy is a closed, author-controlled design, and allowing it to cross module boundaries would let another module insert itself into your closed family, defeating the purpose. So the compiler never lets a permitted subtype live in a different module.

Within a **named module**, the rule relaxes on packages: permitted subtypes may be in **different packages of the same module**. This is because a module is itself a strong encapsulation boundary, so the author already controls everything inside the module. For example, a module `com.bank.accounts` can declare `sealed interface Account` in package `com.bank.accounts.api` and permit `LoanAccount` in package `com.bank.accounts.loan`, as long as both packages are in the same module. This lets you organise a sealed hierarchy across a clean package structure.

On the **classpath**, meaning the unnamed module, the rule is stricter: all permitted subtypes must be in the **same package** as the sealed type. Without a module boundary, the package is the only encapsulation unit the compiler can rely on, so it requires the whole sealed family to sit in one package. If you try to permit a subtype from another package on the classpath, you get a compile error such as "class is in a different package from its sealed supertype."

The practical consequence is that **modularising** your application unlocks cleaner package organisation for sealed hierarchies. A library author shipping a modular JAR can spread a sealed type and its subtypes across several packages for readability, exporting only the API package while keeping subtypes in internal packages. A non-modular application forced onto the classpath must keep the whole family in one package, which can feel cramped for large hierarchies.

A senior nuance is that the permitted subtypes must also be **accessible** to the sealed type at compile time, which interacts with module exports: even within a module the subtypes are visible because module-internal access does not require exporting, but across the module's public API you export only what callers need. Another nuance is that this rule is checked by the compiler and also recorded in the `PermittedSubclasses` class-file attribute, and the JVM re-validates at load time, so you cannot smuggle in a cross-module subtype through bytecode. A final nuance is that this is one more reason real production banking systems adopt JPMS modules: it gives sealed hierarchies both strong encapsulation and flexible package layout, which matters when modelling large closed domains like transaction types or regulatory states.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India wants to model account products as a sealed hierarchy, but for clean architecture it wants the sealed `Account` interface in an `api` package and the concrete products in a `products` package. The bank needs to know whether this cross-package layout is allowed. It is allowed only if everything lives in the same named module. This shows the module rule.

Problem 2 — The bank's older code runs on the plain classpath without modules. There, the same cross-package attempt fails to compile, forcing all subtypes into one package. We show why and the error that results.

Problem 3 — A third-party vendor module tries to add its own permitted subtype to the bank's sealed `Account`. This is impossible because a sealed hierarchy cannot cross modules, protecting the bank's closed product set from outside tampering. We illustrate the boundary.

In the mini-project we present a modular layout where the sealed `Account` is in one package and its permitted subtypes are in another package of the same module, a `module-info.java` describing the module, and a demo that uses the accounts. We explain in comments the classpath restriction and the cross-module prohibition.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The answer is: it depends on modules. The one universal rule is that all permitted subtypes of a sealed type must live in the same module as the sealed type. A sealed hierarchy is a closed, author-controlled family, and letting it cross module boundaries would allow another module to insert itself into my closed set, which defeats the whole point, so the compiler never permits a subtype from a different module.

Within a single named module the rule relaxes on packages, so permitted subtypes may be declared in different packages of that same module. The reason is that the module is itself a strong encapsulation boundary, so I already control everything inside it. In my banking project I put the sealed Account interface in an api package and the concrete products in a products package, and because both packages are in the same account module, the cross-package permits compiles cleanly. I then export only the api package and keep the products package internal, which is nice for architecture.

On the plain classpath, meaning the unnamed module, the rule is stricter: all permitted subtypes must be in the same package as the sealed type. Without a module boundary the package is the only encapsulation unit the compiler can trust, so the whole family must sit in one package, and trying to permit a subtype from another package gives a compile error saying the class is in a different package from its sealed supertype.

The practical lesson I give is that modularising unlocks a cleaner package layout for sealed hierarchies while still keeping them strongly closed, which is exactly what a bank wants for a large closed domain such as account products or transaction states. The module boundary also means an outside vendor module can never inject a new permitted account type into our sealed Account, so our product set stays protected. And because the permitted set is recorded in the class file and re-validated by the JVM at load time, nobody can smuggle in a cross-module subtype through bytecode either.

answers.shortTitle: Is listing all permitted subclasses optional if they're in the same file?

s1_definition.profdef: Yes. If all of a sealed type's permitted direct subtypes are declared in the same source file (the same compilation unit) as the sealed type, the `permits` clause may be omitted. The compiler then infers the permitted set as exactly those subtypes declared in that file. This inference applies to auxiliary top-level classes in the file and to nested classes. If any permitted subtype lives in a different file, the `permits` clause becomes mandatory.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India writes its account-product policy on a single page. If every approved product is also fully described on that very same page, head office does not need to write a separate "approved list" at the top, because anyone reading the page can see the complete set of products right there. But if some approved products are described on other pages kept elsewhere, then head office must write an explicit "approved list" naming them, so readers know the full set without hunting through other documents. One page with everything needs no separate list; scattered pages do.
s1_definition.oneliner: The `permits` clause is optional only when all permitted subtypes are in the same source file, where the compiler infers them automatically.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Yes. If all of a sealed type's permitted direct subtypes are declared in the same source file (the same compilation unit) as the sealed type, the `permits` clause may be omitted. The compiler then infers the permitted set as exactly those subtypes declared in that file. This inference applies to auxiliary top-level classes in the file and to nested classes. If any permitted subtype lives in a different file, the `permits` clause becomes mandatory.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India writes its account-product policy on a single page. If every approved product is also fully described on that very same page, head office does not need to write a separate "approved list" at the top, because anyone reading the page can see the complete set of products right there. But if some approved products are described on other pages kept elsewhere, then head office must write an explicit "approved list" naming them, so readers know the full set without hunting through other documents. One page with everything needs no separate list; scattered pages do.

**One line to remember:** The `permits` clause is optional only when all permitted subtypes are in the same source file, where the compiler infers them automatically.

sections.s2_technical:
When you declare a type `sealed` you normally follow it with a `permits` clause naming the allowed direct subtypes. However, the Java language allows you to **omit `permits`** in one specific case: when every permitted direct subtype is declared in the **same source file** as the sealed type. In that situation the compiler scans the file and infers the permitted set to be exactly the subtypes declared there that directly extend or implement the sealed type.

This works because a single source file is a single compilation unit that the compiler reads in full, so it can see all the subtypes without needing an explicit list. The convenience is real for **small, closed hierarchies** written together. For example, a sealed interface `Shape` with record subtypes `Circle`, `Square`, and `Triangle` all in one file can skip the `permits` clause, and the compiler treats exactly those three as permitted. Adding a fourth subtype in the same file automatically extends the permitted set.

The inference covers both **auxiliary top-level classes** in the file and **nested** types. A single `.java` file may contain one public type and several package-private top-level types; if the sealed type and its subtypes are among these, inference works. It also works when the subtypes are nested inside the sealed type or alongside it. The key requirement is simply that they share the file.

The moment **any permitted subtype is in a different file**, the `permits` clause is **required**. You cannot mix inference and explicit listing: if even one subtype is outside the file, you must write the full `permits` clause naming every permitted direct subtype, including those that happen to be in the same file. So inference is an all-or-nothing convenience tied to co-location in one file.

A senior nuance is that relying on same-file inference couples the hierarchy to a single file, which is fine for small algebraic-data-type-style models but does not scale to large hierarchies that you naturally split across files for readability — there you write an explicit `permits`. Another nuance is that even with inference, each permitted subtype must still carry `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`, because that rule is independent of whether `permits` is written; records satisfy it implicitly by being final. A final nuance is that the inferred permitted set is still recorded in the `PermittedSubclasses` class-file attribute exactly as if you had written it, so at the bytecode level there is no difference — inference is purely a source-level convenience, and the sealing guarantee is identical.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India models a small, fixed set of transaction outcomes as a sealed hierarchy, and the whole model is small enough to live in one file. The bank wants to avoid the boilerplate of repeating the subtype names in a `permits` clause when the compiler can already see them in the same file. This is exactly same-file inference.

Problem 2 — As the model grows, one outcome type must move to its own file for reasons of size. The bank needs to understand that the moment a subtype leaves the file, the `permits` clause becomes mandatory and must name every direct subtype. We show both the inferred version and the explicit version.

Problem 3 — The bank wants to confirm that inference gives exactly the same sealing guarantee as an explicit list, so that an exhaustive switch still works. We demonstrate an exhaustive switch over the inferred sealed set.

In the mini-project we define, in one file, a sealed interface `TransactionResult` with record subtypes `Approved`, `Declined`, and `Pending`, omitting the `permits` clause, then a handler that switches exhaustively over them, logging each. Comments show the explicit `permits` version needed if a subtype moved to another file.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Yes, listing permitted subclasses is optional when all of them are declared in the same source file as the sealed type. In that case I can omit the permits clause entirely, and the compiler infers the permitted set to be exactly those subtypes declared in that file. This works because a single source file is one compilation unit the compiler reads in full, so it can already see the complete set without me repeating it.

This is a genuine convenience for small, closed hierarchies that I write together in one file, which is a common style for algebraic-data-type-style modelling. In my banking project I model transaction results as a sealed interface with three record subtypes, approved, declined, and pending, all in the same file, and I skip the permits clause. The compiler infers those three as the permitted set, and because records are implicitly final they automatically satisfy the rule that every permitted subtype must be final, sealed, or non-sealed.

The important boundary is that inference is all-or-nothing and tied to co-location. The moment any permitted subtype lives in a different file, the permits clause becomes mandatory, and then I must name every direct permitted subtype explicitly, including the ones still in the same file. So if my pending result grew large enough to move into its own file, I would have to add an explicit permits clause naming approved, declined, and pending. For large hierarchies I naturally split across files anyway, so I write permits explicitly there.

What I stress is that inference gives exactly the same guarantee as an explicit list. The inferred permitted set is recorded in the class file in the same PermittedSubclasses attribute, so at the bytecode level there is no difference, and the sealing is just as strong. That means my exhaustive switch over the result types still works with no default branch, and if a teammate adds a new result type in the file, every switch that is not exhaustive fails to compile. So same-file inference is purely a source-level convenience that removes boilerplate without weakening the closed-hierarchy safety a bank relies on.

answers.question: Can a sealed class be abstract, and what is the impact on inheritance?
answers.shortTitle: Can a sealed class be abstract, and what is the impact on inheritance?

s1_definition.profdef: Yes. A sealed class may also be `abstract`. The `sealed` and `abstract` modifiers are orthogonal: `sealed` controls which classes may extend it, while `abstract` controls whether it can be instantiated directly. An abstract sealed class cannot be instantiated and may declare abstract methods, and its concrete behaviour must be provided by its permitted subclasses, each of which must be declared `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`. This combination is the idiomatic way to define a closed family of related concrete types sharing a common abstract base.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India defines an abstract concept of "Account" that describes what every account must do — report its balance, apply monthly processing — but you can never walk in and open a plain "Account"; you must open a specific product. At the same time, head office seals the concept so only three named products may ever be an Account. So "Account" is both a blueprint you cannot instantiate directly (abstract) and a closed family with a fixed membership list (sealed). The two rules work together: a blueprint with a locked guest list.
s1_definition.oneliner: A sealed class can be abstract — `abstract` stops direct instantiation while `sealed` restricts who may extend it, and both constraints apply at once.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Yes. A sealed class may also be `abstract`. The `sealed` and `abstract` modifiers are orthogonal: `sealed` controls which classes may extend it, while `abstract` controls whether it can be instantiated directly. An abstract sealed class cannot be instantiated and may declare abstract methods, and its concrete behaviour must be provided by its permitted subclasses, each of which must be declared `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`. This combination is the idiomatic way to define a closed family of related concrete types sharing a common abstract base.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India defines an abstract concept of "Account" that describes what every account must do — report its balance, apply monthly processing — but you can never walk in and open a plain "Account"; you must open a specific product. At the same time, head office seals the concept so only three named products may ever be an Account. So "Account" is both a blueprint you cannot instantiate directly (abstract) and a closed family with a fixed membership list (sealed). The two rules work together: a blueprint with a locked guest list.

**One line to remember:** A sealed class can be abstract — `abstract` stops direct instantiation while `sealed` restricts who may extend it, and both constraints apply at once.

sections.s2_technical:
`sealed` and `abstract` answer two different questions. `abstract` answers "can I create an instance of this class directly?" — the answer is no, and it allows the class to have abstract methods that subclasses must implement. `sealed` answers "which classes are allowed to extend this class?" — the answer is only the listed permitted subclasses. Because they govern different things, Java lets you combine them freely: `public abstract sealed class Account permits SavingsAccount, CurrentAccount, LoanAccount { ... }`.

An **abstract sealed class** is extremely common and idiomatic. You use it when there is shared state and behaviour across a closed set of concrete types. The abstract base holds the common fields and concrete helper methods, declares abstract methods for the parts that vary, and the sealing guarantees that only your known subclasses exist. Each permitted subclass still must be `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`, exactly as for any sealed type.

The **impact on inheritance** is twofold. First, because the base is abstract, no code can do `new Account(...)`; callers must create one of the concrete permitted subclasses. This pushes all instantiation to the leaves, which is usually what you want for a type family. Second, because the base is sealed, the set of subclasses is fixed and known to the compiler, so the abstract methods have a finite, known set of implementations. This enables exhaustive handling: a `switch` over the abstract sealed type can cover every subclass without a `default`, and the compiler verifies completeness.

A subtle point is the interaction with **abstract methods and exhaustiveness**. You can implement varying behaviour either by overriding an abstract method in each subclass (classic polymorphism) or by pattern-switching on the sealed type in a service. Both are valid. Overriding keeps behaviour with the data; switching centralises behaviour in one place and benefits from compiler-checked exhaustiveness. In banking you often use both: core invariants as abstract methods on the base, and cross-cutting policies as exhaustive switches in services.

A senior nuance is that an abstract sealed class can still have **constructors**, which the subclasses call via `super`, letting you enforce invariants on common fields even though the base cannot be instantiated alone. Another nuance is that if you make the base `sealed` but **not** abstract, it can be instantiated and extended by its permitted subclasses, which is occasionally useful but less common than the abstract form. A final nuance is that an abstract sealed class combined with final record or final class leaves is the cleanest Java encoding of an algebraic data type, giving you a non-instantiable, closed, polymorphic family that the compiler fully understands — ideal for modelling a bank's fixed set of account products or transaction states with strong guarantees.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India wants a common `Account` base that holds shared fields like id, holder, and balance, and defines shared behaviour like crediting money, while forbidding anyone from creating a plain, typeless account. The base must be abstract so only real products can be opened. This is the abstract part.

Problem 2 — The bank also wants to guarantee that only savings, current, and loan products can ever be accounts, so no rogue subtype appears. The base must be sealed with a permits list. This is the sealed part, and together they form an abstract sealed class.

Problem 3 — Interest calculation varies by product, so the base declares an abstract `monthlyInterest` method that each concrete subclass implements, and a service also runs an exhaustive switch to apply a regulatory cap, demonstrating both overriding and exhaustive switching over the sealed family.

In the mini-project we define `abstract sealed class Account permits SavingsAccount, CurrentAccount, LoanAccount`, with shared fields, a constructor, a concrete `credit` method, and an abstract `monthlyInterest`. The three final subclasses implement it, and a service applies an exhaustive switch, logging each computation.

The code contains: the abstract sealed base, three final subclasses, an `InterestService`, and a demo.

Yes, a sealed class can also be abstract, because sealed and abstract control two different things. Abstract controls whether the class can be instantiated directly, and the answer is no, plus it allows abstract methods that subclasses must implement. Sealed controls which classes are allowed to extend it, limiting them to the permitted list. Since they govern different concerns, Java lets me combine them, and the abstract sealed class is actually the most idiomatic form.

I use an abstract sealed class whenever there is shared state and behaviour across a closed set of concrete types. The abstract base holds the common fields and concrete helper methods, declares abstract methods for the parts that vary, and the sealing guarantees only my known subclasses exist. A nice detail is that the abstract base can still have constructors that the subclasses call through super, so I can enforce invariants on the shared fields even though the base itself can never be instantiated.

answers.question: How does sealing improve `instanceof` checks and exhaustive `switch` pattern matching?
answers.shortTitle: How does sealing improve `instanceof` checks and exhaustive `switch` pattern matching?

s1_definition.profdef: Sealing gives the compiler complete knowledge of the finite set of subtypes of a type. This lets a `switch` over a sealed type be checked for exhaustiveness: if every permitted subtype is covered, the switch needs no `default` branch, and if a subtype is missing, compilation fails. Combined with pattern matching, `instanceof` and `switch` patterns become safer because the compiler can reason about the closed set, enabling exhaustive type-based dispatch without a fallback and catching unhandled cases at compile time rather than at runtime.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India has a fixed, closed list of exactly three account products. Because the list is closed and head office knows every entry, a clerk processing accounts can write a checklist with one row per product and be certain the checklist is complete — there is no mysterious fourth product that could slip through unhandled. If someone later adds a fourth product to the official list, every checklist in the bank that is now incomplete is immediately flagged for update. Sealing is what makes the list closed and known, so the checklists can be provably complete.
s1_definition.oneliner: Sealing makes the subtype set finite and known, so the compiler can prove a `switch` is exhaustive and force you to handle every case without a `default`.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Sealing gives the compiler complete knowledge of the finite set of subtypes of a type. This lets a `switch` over a sealed type be checked for exhaustiveness: if every permitted subtype is covered, the switch needs no `default` branch, and if a subtype is missing, compilation fails. Combined with pattern matching, `instanceof` and `switch` patterns become safer because the compiler can reason about the closed set, enabling exhaustive type-based dispatch without a fallback and catching unhandled cases at compile time rather than at runtime.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India has a fixed, closed list of exactly three account products. Because the list is closed and head office knows every entry, a clerk processing accounts can write a checklist with one row per product and be certain the checklist is complete — there is no mysterious fourth product that could slip through unhandled. If someone later adds a fourth product to the official list, every checklist in the bank that is now incomplete is immediately flagged for update. Sealing is what makes the list closed and known, so the checklists can be provably complete.

**One line to remember:** Sealing makes the subtype set finite and known, so the compiler can prove a `switch` is exhaustive and force you to handle every case without a `default`.

sections.s2_technical:
Before sealed types, a type could be extended by anyone, anywhere, so the compiler could never be sure it knew all subtypes. That meant a `switch` or chain of `instanceof` checks over subtypes always needed a `default` or `else` to handle "some unknown subtype," even if you believed you had covered them all. If a new subtype appeared, the `default` would silently swallow it, often causing a subtle runtime bug.

**Sealing changes this** by giving the compiler the complete, finite list of permitted subtypes. Now when you write a `switch` over a sealed type with a case for each permitted subtype, the compiler can verify that **every** possible subtype is handled, which is called **exhaustiveness checking**. If the switch is exhaustive, you do **not** need a `default` branch. For example, a `switch` on a sealed `Account` with cases for `SavingsAccount`, `CurrentAccount`, and `LoanAccount` is complete, and the compiler accepts it without `default`.

The real power appears when the **sealed set changes**. If a developer adds a new permitted subtype to the sealed type, every exhaustive `switch` that does not handle the new subtype now **fails to compile**. This turns a dangerous runtime gap into a compile-time error, so the compiler itself reminds you to update every place that dispatches on the type. In a bank, where forgetting to handle a new account product or transaction state could cause financial errors, this guarantee is extremely valuable.

For **`instanceof` with pattern matching**, sealing helps the compiler reason about type coverage. Pattern matching for `instanceof` lets you write `if (a instanceof SavingsAccount s) { ... }` and bind `s` directly. When this is used in an if-else chain over a sealed type, while the language still requires a final `else` for an if-chain, the closed set documents and bounds the possibilities, and modern `switch` patterns supersede the chain with true exhaustiveness. Switch patterns also support **guarded patterns** and **null handling**, and over a sealed type the compiler knows the universe of cases, enabling precise, safe dispatch.

A senior nuance is that exhaustiveness interacts with **sealed hierarchies that are multi-level**: if a permitted subtype is itself sealed, the compiler expands the set transitively, so you can either switch on the intermediate sealed type or on its leaves, and exhaustiveness is computed over the full closed tree. Another nuance is that if you do add a `default` to an exhaustive sealed switch, you lose the compile-time safety net, because the `default` would absorb any new subtype silently, so for sealed types you deliberately omit `default` to keep the guarantee. A final nuance is that this pairing of sealed types with pattern-matching switches is Java's realisation of algebraic-data-type pattern matching found in functional languages, giving banking domain models both closed-set safety and concise, exhaustive dispatch, which reduces whole classes of "unhandled case" defects.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India dispatches different logic based on the transaction result type, and in the past used a `default` branch that silently mishandled any new result type, causing a production incident. The bank wants the compiler to force every dispatch site to handle every result. Sealing plus an exhaustive switch provides this.

Problem 2 — The bank needs type-based extraction of data from each result, such as the amount from an approved result or the reason from a declined one, done safely without casts. Pattern matching in the switch binds the concrete type and its record components directly, avoiding manual casting and the risk of `ClassCastException`.

Problem 3 — The bank wants a guarantee that when a new result type is introduced later, the build breaks at every switch that does not handle it, so nothing is missed. We show that removing a case causes a compile error, proving the safety net.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Sealing improves instanceof and switch pattern matching by giving the compiler complete knowledge of the finite set of subtypes. Before sealed types, any type could be extended by anyone, so the compiler could never be sure it knew all subtypes, which meant a switch or an instanceof chain over subtypes always needed a default or else to cover some unknown subtype, and that default would silently swallow any new subtype and cause subtle runtime bugs.

With sealing, the compiler has the exact, closed list of permitted subtypes, so it can check exhaustiveness. When my switch has a case for each permitted subtype, the compiler verifies that every possibility is covered, and I do not need a default branch at all. In my banking project my transaction result is a sealed interface with approved, declined, and pending record subtypes, and my dispatcher switches over all three with no default, which compiles precisely because it is provably complete.

The real power shows up when the set changes. If a teammate adds a new permitted subtype, every exhaustive switch that does not handle it now fails to compile, so the compiler itself points me to every dispatch site that needs updating. That turns a dangerous runtime gap into a compile-time error, which in a bank is enormously valuable because forgetting to handle a new transaction state or account product could cause financial errors. For that reason I deliberately omit the default on a sealed switch, because adding one would hide the safety net by absorbing new subtypes silently.

Pattern matching makes it even better. With record patterns I bind the components directly in each case, so I extract the amount from an approved result or the reason from a declined one without any cast and without risk of a class-cast exception, since the match tests and binds in one step. I also use guarded patterns with when to refine within the closed set, for example routing high-value approvals to a compliance branch. So the combination of sealed types and pattern-matching switches gives me closed-set safety and concise, exhaustive dispatch, which eliminates a whole class of unhandled-case defects, and it is Java's version of the algebraic-data-type pattern matching you see in functional languages.

answers.question: Can a sealed class permit itself?
answers.shortTitle: Can a sealed class permit itself?

s1_definition.profdef: No. A sealed class cannot list itself in its own `permits` clause. The `permits` clause names the *direct subtypes* allowed to extend the sealed type, and a type cannot be its own subtype — a class cannot extend itself. Attempting `sealed class Account permits Account` is a compile error because it is cyclic and meaningless. A sealed non-abstract class can itself be instantiated as a leaf, but that is different from permitting itself; it simply means the sealed class is concrete.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India's head office writes the closed list of products that may be "a kind of Account." Putting "Account" itself on that list makes no sense, because the list is meant to name the specific products that are types of Account, not the concept of Account repeating itself. A category cannot be a member of its own membership list — that is circular and empty of meaning. So head office never writes the concept's own name on the list of its approved variants.
s1_definition.oneliner: A sealed class cannot permit itself because `permits` lists direct subtypes, and nothing can be its own subtype.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** No. A sealed class cannot list itself in its own `permits` clause. The `permits` clause names the *direct subtypes* allowed to extend the sealed type, and a type cannot be its own subtype — a class cannot extend itself. Attempting `sealed class Account permits Account` is a compile error because it is cyclic and meaningless. A sealed non-abstract class can itself be instantiated as a leaf, but that is different from permitting itself; it simply means the sealed class is concrete.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India's head office writes the closed list of products that may be "a kind of Account." Putting "Account" itself on that list makes no sense, because the list is meant to name the specific products that are types of Account, not the concept of Account repeating itself. A category cannot be a member of its own membership list — that is circular and empty of meaning. So head office never writes the concept's own name on the list of its approved variants.

**One line to remember:** A sealed class cannot permit itself because `permits` lists direct subtypes, and nothing can be its own subtype.

sections.s2_technical:
The `permits` clause declares the set of **direct subtypes** that may extend or implement the sealed type. By definition a subtype is a *different* type that inherits from the sealed type. A class cannot extend itself — Java forbids a class being its own superclass, directly or through a cycle — so a sealed type can never appear in its own `permits` list. Writing `sealed class Account permits Account {}` produces a **compile error** about a cyclic or invalid permitted subtype, because `Account extends Account` is not a valid relationship.

This is sometimes confused with a related but different question: can a sealed class itself be a **concrete, instantiable type** that participates in the hierarchy as a value? The answer there is yes, but it has nothing to do with permitting itself. If a sealed class is **not abstract**, it can be instantiated directly, so the sealed class is itself a usable leaf value in addition to having permitted subclasses. For example `sealed class Node permits Branch {}` where `Node` is concrete means you can create a `Node` and also a `Branch`, but `Node` did not permit itself — it permitted `Branch`, and it is usable on its own because it is non-abstract.

Another nearby confusion is a **recursive data structure**, such as a tree where a node contains references to other nodes of the same sealed type. That is fine and common: the sealed type can have fields of its own type, and subtypes can reference the sealed supertype. Recursion in the data (a node holding child nodes) is completely different from a type permitting itself in its `permits` clause. The former is normal composition; the latter is an illegal inheritance cycle.

The rule also connects to how sealing is recorded. The permitted set goes into the `PermittedSubclasses` class-file attribute, listing the direct subclasses. The sealed class's own entry is never in that list because the attribute describes who may extend it, not the class itself. The JVM validates at load time that each permitted entry is a genuine direct subclass, and a self-reference would fail that validation just as it fails compilation.

A senior nuance is that this reflects a general principle: inheritance forms a **directed acyclic graph** rooted at `Object`, and any cycle, including a one-node self-cycle, is forbidden throughout Java, not just for sealed types. Another nuance is that if you want the sealed type to be usable as a value and also closed, you make it a **non-abstract sealed class** with permitted subtypes, which gives you a concrete base plus a closed set of specialisations, but you still never list the base in its own permits. A final nuance is that for modelling, if you find yourself wanting a type to permit itself, it usually signals you actually want either a concrete sealed base or a recursive field, and recognising that keeps the design clean in a banking domain model.

Problem 1 — A developer at National Bank of India mistakenly tries to write a sealed `Account` that permits itself, thinking it would let `Account` be both the base and a usable value. We need to show this does not compile and explain why, so the team understands the rule.

The correct solution is a **non-abstract sealed class** that permits its real subtypes while being instantiable itself, which we demonstrate with a sealed `LedgerNode` that is concrete and permits a `SummaryNode`.

Problem 3 — The team also wants a recursive structure where a node references other nodes of the same type, which is often mistaken for self-permitting. We show a sealed `TransactionNode` holding a list of child `TransactionNode` values, proving recursion in data is fine and unrelated to permits.

No, a sealed class cannot permit itself. The permits clause names the direct subtypes allowed to extend the sealed type, and by definition a subtype is a different type that inherits from it. A class cannot extend itself, and Java forbids any inheritance cycle, so writing a sealed Account that permits Account is a compile error about a cyclic or invalid permitted subtype. There are two nearby ideas that people confuse with self-permitting, and I like to clear both up. The first is whether a sealed class can itself be a usable, instantiable value. In my project a transaction node holds a list of child transaction nodes and sums them recursively. The underlying principle I mention is that Java's inheritance forms a directed acyclic graph rooted at Object, so any cycle, including a one-node self-cycle, is forbidden everywhere, not only for sealed types. answers.question: What happens if a permitted subclass has no `final`/`sealed`/`non-sealed` modifier?
answers.shortTitle: What happens if a permitted subclass has no `final`/`sealed`/`non-sealed` modifier?

s1_definition.profdef: It is a compile error. Every class or interface that directly extends or implements a sealed type is required to specify its own extensibility by being declared exactly one of `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`. If a permitted subclass omits all three modifiers, the compiler rejects the code with an error stating that a sealed class's subclass must be final, sealed, or non-sealed. The one exception is records and enums, which are implicitly final and therefore satisfy the rule automatically. This requirement forces the author to make a deliberate decision about whether the sealing continues, ends, or is reopened at each subtype.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India approves a product to be a kind of Account. Head office insists that each approved product must stamp its own policy on further variations: either "no further variants allowed" (final), "only my own named variants allowed" (sealed), or "anyone may add variants freely" (non-sealed). A product that forgets to stamp any policy is sent back — the form is incomplete, and head office refuses to file it. The bank will not accept an approved product that leaves its extension policy blank.
s1_definition.oneliner: A permitted subclass must declare `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`; omitting all three is a compile error, because sealing requires an explicit extensibility decision at every subtype.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** It is a compile error. Every class or interface that directly extends or implements a sealed type is required to specify its own extensibility by being declared exactly one of `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`. If a permitted subclass omits all three modifiers, the compiler rejects the code with an error stating that a sealed class's subclass must be final, sealed, or non-sealed. The one exception is records and enums, which are implicitly final and therefore satisfy the rule automatically. This requirement forces the author to make a deliberate decision about whether the sealing continues, ends, or is reopened at each subtype.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India approves a product to be a kind of Account. Head office insists that each approved product must stamp its own policy on further variations: either "no further variants allowed" (final), "only my own named variants allowed" (sealed), or "anyone may add variants freely" (non-sealed). A product that forgets to stamp any policy is sent back — the form is incomplete, and head office refuses to file it. The bank will not accept an approved product that leaves its extension policy blank.

**One line to remember:** A permitted subclass must declare `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`; omitting all three is a compile error, because sealing requires an explicit extensibility decision at every subtype.

sections.s2_technical:
When a type is sealed, it closes its hierarchy at the first level by naming its permitted subtypes. But sealing must not leak: if a permitted subtype could be extended freely without saying so, the hierarchy would no longer be closed, because unknown classes could slip in beneath that subtype. To prevent this, Java **requires every permitted subtype to state its own extensibility** explicitly, choosing exactly one of three modifiers.

**`final`** ends the hierarchy at that subtype: no class may extend it, so that branch of the closed family is a leaf. This is the most common choice for concrete products. **`sealed`** continues the closure: the subtype itself becomes sealed and must provide its own `permits` list (or rely on same-file inference), extending the closed hierarchy another level. **`non-sealed`** deliberately reopens that branch: the subtype may be extended by any class without restriction, punching a controlled hole in the sealing where you have decided extensibility is desirable, such as a base for third-party plugins.

If a permitted subtype **omits all three**, the compiler emits an error like "sealed, non-sealed or final modifiers expected." The compiler cannot guess your intent — leaving it blank would create an ambiguous, half-open hierarchy — so it forces the decision. This is a deliberate language design choice that makes extensibility an explicit, reviewed property of every subtype rather than an accident.

The important **exceptions** are types that are already implicitly final. A **record** is implicitly `final`, so a record that implements a sealed interface satisfies the rule without writing `final`. An **enum** is effectively final as well (its constants are fixed), so an enum implementing a sealed interface is fine. In these cases you do not add a modifier because the type's nature already closes it. For ordinary classes and interfaces, though, you must write one of the three.

A subtle point for **interfaces**: a sealed interface's permitted subtype that is itself an interface must be `sealed` or `non-sealed` (interfaces cannot be `final`), while a permitted subtype that is a class follows the class rules of `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`. So the exact allowed modifier set depends on whether the subtype is a class or an interface, but the principle is identical: the extensibility must be explicit.

A senior nuance is that this requirement is what makes the **closed-set guarantee hold transitively**: because every subtype must declare final, sealed, or non-sealed, the compiler can compute the complete leaf set for exhaustiveness checking, and a `non-sealed` branch is the one place where that set becomes open, which the compiler accounts for by then requiring a `default` or wildcard when switching if the open branch is reachable. Another nuance is that forgetting the modifier is a frequent first-time error, and the fix is simply to decide and declare it. A final nuance is that in a banking domain this explicitness is valuable because it forces an architectural decision at each product type about whether future variants are allowed, which is exactly the kind of deliberate design a regulated system benefits from.

Problem 2 — The team then decides the correct policy for each product: savings and current are leaves and must be `final`, loan has further sub-products so it is `sealed`, and one promotional line must stay open for future add-ons so it is `non-sealed`. We implement each with the right modifier.

sections.s6_takeaway:
If a permitted subclass has no final, sealed, or non-sealed modifier, it is a compile error. The language requires every class or interface that directly extends or implements a sealed type to declare its own extensibility by being exactly one of those three, and leaving all three off produces an error saying sealed, non-sealed, or final modifiers are expected. The compiler refuses to guess my intent, so it forces a deliberate decision at every subtype.

The reason is that sealing must not leak. A sealed type closes its hierarchy at the first level by naming permitted subtypes, but if one of those subtypes could then be extended freely without saying so, unknown classes could slip in beneath it and the hierarchy would no longer be closed. So each permitted subtype states its policy: final means the branch ends there with no further extension, sealed means it continues the closure with its own permits list, and non-sealed means it deliberately reopens that branch for unrestricted extension, which is a controlled hole I use for something like a plugin base.

There is an important exception I always mention: records and enums are implicitly final, so a record or enum that implements a sealed interface satisfies the rule automatically without any modifier. In my banking project I use a record for a settlement result that implements a sealed settlement interface, and it compiles cleanly with no extra keyword because it is already final. For ordinary classes and interfaces, though, I must write one of the three, and for a permitted subtype that is itself an interface the choice is sealed or non-sealed because interfaces cannot be final.

In my account model savings and current are final leaves, loan is sealed with its own permitted home-loan leaf, and a promotional line is non-sealed so it can take future add-ons. The value of this rule in a bank is that it turns extensibility into an explicit, reviewed architectural decision at each product type rather than an accident, and it is exactly what keeps the closed-set guarantee holding transitively so my exhaustive switches stay sound. So the short answer is: declare final, sealed, or non-sealed at every permitted subtype, or the build fails, and that is by design.

answers.question: Can you serialize/deserialize a sealed hierarchy with Jackson/Gson, and what are the caveats?
answers.shortTitle: Can you serialize/deserialize a sealed hierarchy with Jackson/Gson, and what are the caveats?

s1_definition.profdef: Yes, a sealed hierarchy can be serialized and deserialized with Jackson or Gson, but polymorphic deserialization requires type information to be present in the JSON so the library can pick the correct permitted subtype. Jackson supports this cleanly through `@JsonTypeInfo` and `@JsonSubTypes`, and modern Jackson can even infer permitted subtypes from the sealed `permits` list. Gson needs a registered `RuntimeTypeAdapterFactory` or a custom adapter because Gson has no built-in polymorphic support. The main caveats are embedding a type discriminator, keeping the registered or annotated subtype set in sync with the sealed `permits`, and handling records (common sealed leaves) which need constructor-based binding.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India sends account documents between systems as forms (JSON). Reading a form back is easy if the form has a clear label at the top saying which exact product it is — "Savings," "Current," or "Loan" — so the clerk knows which specific form template to use. Without that label, the clerk sees the fields but cannot be sure which product it is, and may fill in the wrong template. Serialization writes the form; deserialization reads it back; and the type label is the discriminator that tells the reader which permitted product to reconstruct.
s1_definition.oneliner: Yes — serialize freely, but polymorphic deserialization needs a type discriminator in the JSON, via Jackson's `@JsonTypeInfo`/`@JsonSubTypes` or Gson's `RuntimeTypeAdapterFactory`.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Yes, a sealed hierarchy can be serialized and deserialized with Jackson or Gson, but polymorphic deserialization requires type information to be present in the JSON so the library can pick the correct permitted subtype. Jackson supports this cleanly through `@JsonTypeInfo` and `@JsonSubTypes`, and modern Jackson can even infer permitted subtypes from the sealed `permits` list. Gson needs a registered `RuntimeTypeAdapterFactory` or a custom adapter because Gson has no built-in polymorphic support. The main caveats are embedding a type discriminator, keeping the registered or annotated subtype set in sync with the sealed `permits`, and handling records (common sealed leaves) which need constructor-based binding.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India sends account documents between systems as forms (JSON). Reading a form back is easy if the form has a clear label at the top saying which exact product it is — "Savings," "Current," or "Loan" — so the clerk knows which specific form template to use. Without that label, the clerk sees the fields but cannot be sure which product it is, and may fill in the wrong template. Serialization writes the form; deserialization reads it back; and the type label is the discriminator that tells the reader which permitted product to reconstruct.

**One line to remember:** Yes — serialize freely, but polymorphic deserialization needs a type discriminator in the JSON, via Jackson's `@JsonTypeInfo`/`@JsonSubTypes` or Gson's `RuntimeTypeAdapterFactory`.

sections.s2_technical:
**Serialization** (object to JSON) of a sealed hierarchy is straightforward because the library just reads the concrete object's fields. The challenge is **deserialization** (JSON back to object) when the declared type is the sealed supertype: the library receives JSON and must decide which permitted subtype to instantiate, and plain field data alone is often ambiguous. The solution is to include a **type discriminator** in the JSON — a property whose value names the subtype — so the library can route to the correct class.

In **Jackson**, you enable this with `@JsonTypeInfo(use = Id.NAME, property = "type")` on the sealed type and `@JsonSubTypes` listing the mappings, for example `@JsonSubTypes.Type(value = SavingsAccount.class, name = "SAVINGS")`. Then JSON like `{"type":"SAVINGS","id":"SAV2001","balance":1000000}` deserializes into a `SavingsAccount`. A modern convenience is that recent Jackson versions can **infer the subtypes from the sealed `permits` clause**, reducing the need to list them manually, though you still choose the discriminator strategy. Jackson handles **records** well through their canonical constructor, which is important because sealed leaves are frequently records.

In **Gson**, there is **no built-in polymorphic deserialization**, so you must register a `RuntimeTypeAdapterFactory` (from the `gson-extras` companion) that maps a discriminator value to each subtype: `RuntimeTypeAdapterFactory.of(Account.class, "type").registerSubtype(SavingsAccount.class, "SAVINGS")...`. You register it on the `GsonBuilder`. Without this, Gson deserializing into the sealed supertype cannot know the concrete type and fails or produces wrong results. Gson also does not natively bind to record canonical constructors in older versions, so records may need a custom adapter or a recent Gson release.

The **caveats** are the heart of the answer. First, you must **embed a discriminator** and agree on its name and values with every producer and consumer of the JSON. Second, the set of **subtypes known to the serializer must match the sealed `permits`**: if someone adds a permitted subtype but forgets to register or annotate it, deserialization of that new type fails at runtime — a gap the compiler cannot catch for the external JSON boundary. Third, **records as leaves** require constructor binding and have no setters, so the library must support canonical constructors. Fourth, **security**: never enable Jackson default typing that accepts arbitrary class names from JSON, because that is a well-known deserialization vulnerability; use the controlled `Id.NAME` mapping, which only permits your known subtypes — especially critical in banking.

A senior nuance is that sealing actually **helps** here conceptually, because the closed `permits` list is the exact, authoritative set the serializer must support, so you can derive or validate the registered subtypes against it, and Jackson's inference leans on this. Another nuance is **versioning**: when the JSON crosses service boundaries, adding a new permitted subtype is a wire-compatibility change that old consumers cannot deserialize, so you manage it like any schema evolution. A final nuance is that for internal, trusted JSON you can rely on Jackson's permits inference, but for external or cross-organisation JSON you keep an explicit, reviewed discriminator mapping to stay safe and stable.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India sends account objects between microservices as JSON, and the receiving service declares the field as the sealed `Account` supertype. When it reads the JSON it must reconstruct the exact product. Without a type label the service cannot tell a savings account from a current account. We add a discriminator and configure Jackson to route correctly.

Problem 2 — A partner integration uses Gson instead of Jackson, which has no built-in polymorphic support, so the bank must register a `RuntimeTypeAdapterFactory` mapping the discriminator to each permitted subtype. We show that configuration.

Problem 3 — The bank wants safety: it must never allow arbitrary class names in incoming JSON to be instantiated, because that is a deserialization attack vector. We use controlled name-based mapping limited to the known permitted subtypes.

In the mini-project we define a sealed `Account` with Jackson annotations and permitted record subtypes, serialize and deserialize with Jackson, then show the equivalent Gson `RuntimeTypeAdapterFactory` setup in a method, logging the round-trips.

answers.question: How do sealed classes help implement algebraic data types (ADTs)?
answers.shortTitle: How do sealed classes help implement algebraic data types (ADTs)?

s1_definition.profdef: An algebraic data type is a type formed by combining other types, principally as a *sum type* (a value is exactly one of several named variants) and a *product type* (a value bundles several fields together). Sealed types give Java sum types: a sealed interface or class with a closed set of permitted subtypes models "one of these variants," and records model product types by bundling fields. Together, sealed types plus records plus exhaustive pattern-matching `switch` give Java a complete, type-safe encoding of ADTs, with the compiler enforcing that every variant is handled.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India describes a payment outcome as being exactly one of a fixed set of shapes: it is a Success carrying an amount, or a Failure carrying a reason, or a Pending carrying an expected date — never two at once, and never some unknown fourth shape. A sealed type is how the bank writes down that closed "it is exactly one of these" list (the sum), and a record is how each shape bundles its own data (the product). When a clerk processes an outcome, a checklist with one row per shape is guaranteed complete, so no outcome is ever mishandled. That closed "one of these bundles" model is an algebraic data type.
s1_definition.oneliner: Sealed types provide the closed sum ("one of these variants"), records provide the product (bundled fields), and exhaustive `switch` makes handling them type-safe and complete.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** An algebraic data type is a type formed by combining other types, principally as a *sum type* (a value is exactly one of several named variants) and a *product type* (a value bundles several fields together). Sealed types give Java sum types: a sealed interface or class with a closed set of permitted subtypes models "one of these variants," and records model product types by bundling fields. Together, sealed types plus records plus exhaustive pattern-matching `switch` give Java a complete, type-safe encoding of ADTs, with the compiler enforcing that every variant is handled.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India describes a payment outcome as being exactly one of a fixed set of shapes: it is a Success carrying an amount, or a Failure carrying a reason, or a Pending carrying an expected date — never two at once, and never some unknown fourth shape. A sealed type is how the bank writes down that closed "it is exactly one of these" list (the sum), and a record is how each shape bundles its own data (the product). When a clerk processes an outcome, a checklist with one row per shape is guaranteed complete, so no outcome is ever mishandled. That closed "one of these bundles" model is an algebraic data type.

**One line to remember:** Sealed types provide the closed sum ("one of these variants"), records provide the product (bundled fields), and exhaustive `switch` makes handling them type-safe and complete.

sections.s2_technical:
An **algebraic data type** has two building blocks. A **product type** is a bundle of fields, like a pair or a struct — in Java a `record` is exactly this, combining several component values into one immutable type. A **sum type** (also called a tagged union or variant type) says a value is exactly one of several alternatives — this is what Java lacked a clean way to express until sealed types. Combining sums of products is what "algebraic" means: the set of possible values is built by adding up alternatives, each of which multiplies together its fields.

**Sealed types deliver the sum.** A `sealed interface Result permits Success, Failure, Pending` declares that a `Result` is exactly one of three variants, and the `permits` clause closes the set so no other variant can exist. Each variant is typically a **record** (the product part), bundling that variant's own fields, for example `record Success(BigDecimal amount)` and `record Failure(String reason)`. Because records are implicitly final, they satisfy the sealed-subtype rule automatically. This gives a precise, closed "sum of products" exactly like ADTs in functional languages such as Haskell or Scala.

The third ingredient is **exhaustive pattern matching**. A `switch` over the sealed type with a case per variant, using record patterns to destructure the fields, is checked by the compiler for completeness, so you cannot forget a variant and you do not need a `default`. This is the "safe consumption" side of ADTs: defining the data as a closed sum is only half the value; the other half is that every place that consumes it is forced to handle all cases. If you add a variant, every non-exhaustive switch fails to compile.

This pattern shines for modelling **domain states and results**. Instead of a single mutable class with nullable fields and a status enum — where illegal combinations like "status is SUCCESS but reason is set" are possible — an ADT makes **illegal states unrepresentable**: a `Success` simply has no `reason` field, and a `Failure` simply has no `amount` field. The type system prevents the invalid combinations that a flat class would allow. In banking this eliminates a whole category of bugs around half-populated objects.

A senior nuance is that ADTs encourage **total functions**: a function that maps every variant to a result, verified exhaustive by the compiler, which is far safer than scattered `instanceof` chains or status flags. Another nuance is that sealed-plus-records ADTs compose recursively, letting you model trees and expression grammars, such as a sealed `Expr permits Add, Mul, Literal`, which is the classic interpreter pattern done type-safely. A final nuance is that ADTs pair naturally with immutable records for thread-safe, value-based domain modelling, which suits a bank's need for auditable, side-effect-free representations of money states, and the exhaustiveness guarantee means regulatory changes that add a new state are caught at compile time everywhere they must be handled.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India represents the outcome of a payment as one of exactly three shapes: a success with a settled amount, a failure with a reason, or a pending with an expected date. In the past the bank used one class with a status enum and nullable amount and reason fields, which allowed invalid combinations and caused bugs. We model it as a sealed sum of record products so illegal states cannot be represented.

Problem 2 — Every consumer of a payment outcome must handle all three shapes. We use an exhaustive pattern switch with record destructuring so the compiler guarantees completeness, and adding a future shape would break the build at every unhandled site.

Problem 3 — The bank also models a small expression ADT for fee formulas — add, multiply, literal — to show the recursive, interpreter-style power of sealed-plus-records ADTs, evaluating a formula safely.

In the mini-project we define a sealed `PaymentOutcome` with record variants `Success`, `Failure`, and `Pending`, an exhaustive handler, and a recursive sealed `Expr` with `Literal`, `Add`, `Mul` plus an evaluator, logging results.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three payment outcomes — a success of 50,000, a failure for insufficient funds, a pending with an expected date — and a fee formula (1000 + 500) times 2.

Step 1 — The sealed `PaymentOutcome` declares that an outcome is exactly one of three record variants. Each record carries only its own fields, so a success has an amount but no reason, and a failure has a reason but no amount. This makes invalid combinations impossible to construct, unlike a flat class with nullable fields.

Step 2 — The handler's `message` method runs an exhaustive `switch` with record patterns. Because the type is sealed, the compiler verifies all three variants are covered and needs no `default`. Each case destructures the record directly into its fields.

Step 3 — The success case prints the reference and settled amount, the failure case prints the reference and reason, and the pending case prints the reference and expected date. Each outcome is handled totally and safely.

Step 4 — The recursive `Expr` ADT models a fee formula as a tree: a multiply of an add of two literals and another literal. The static `eval` method switches over the three expression variants, recursing into sub-expressions.

Step 5 — Evaluation computes 1000 plus 500 to get 1500, then multiplies by 2 to get 3000, using `BigDecimal`. The result is logged. This shows the interpreter pattern done with full compile-time exhaustiveness, impossible to get a missing-case bug.
